newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya T-bills auction falls on political unrest.
newsitem.headline: Kenya T-bills auction falls on political unrest.

text.p: Kenya's weekly auction of treasury bills took a beating on Thursday, following a pattern set by the currency and the Nairobi bourse after political unrest hit the east African nation.
Central bank officials said the bank auctioned up to 5.074 billion shillings ($87.9 million) of treasury bills on Thursday, down from 5.615 billion shillings last week.
The auctioned total was a far cry from the bank's target of 11 billion shillings.

A senior bank official, who declined to be named, told Reuters that many foreign investors usually attracted to the Kenyan market because of high yields and stability had declined to roll-over their bills due to political uncertainty.

Of the benchmark 91-day t-bills, the bank said it sold 3.781 billion shillings of treasury bills at an average yield of 18.471 percent compared to 2.977 billion shillings at 18.720 percent last Thursday.
The bank said it sold 1.294 billion shillings at an average yield of 19.438 percent of the 182-day category compared to 2.637 billion shillings at an average yield of 19.545 percent.
The bank invited tenders for up to 12 billion shillings of treasury bills for next week's auction on Thursday. But economic analysts said performance will largely depend on the political climate.
Earlier on Thursday, the Kenyan shilling took a further beating driven down by panic-triggered demand for dollars after the worst political violence since pluralist politics returned in 1991.
Commercial bank dealers said even a central bank intervention could not stem a weakening shilling.
The central bank posted a mean shilling rate of 56.38 against the dollar from 55.87 on Wednesday. Against the pound, the shilling was posted at a mean of 95.10 from 94.26.
Dealers said the shilling slipped to 56.80/57.80 in the morning session from an opening of 56.17/56.59.

Kenya, East Africa's economic engine and usually an oasis of stability, saw opposition groups, backed by churches and university students, demanding sweeping constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections later this year.
The violent protests for political reforms in Kenya have upset investors, and many are so wary of this emerging market that turnover on the Nairobi stock exchange has slumped to a year low.

Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the worst clashes between police and protesters since a violent campaign in July 1990 that helped persuade President Daniel arap Moi to allow multi-party politics. ($ = 57.7 Kenyan Shillings)
